questions.prompt: Stock D moves exactly like stock B but twice as far each day. The correlation of A and B is 0.96. What is the correlation of A and D?
options: 1.92, because D moves twice as far
0.48, because D is twice as volatile
questions.explanation: Doubling D doubles both the covariance and D's volatility. Correlation divides one by the other, so the 2 cancels and the value stays 0.96.

questions.prompt: Two stocks have a correlation of 0.98 in their daily returns. What can you conclude?
options: Their prices will stay close together over the next year
Their daily returns move in nearly perfect step, but their prices can still drift apart
One stock causes the other to move
questions.explanation: Correlation describes daily moves. In the simulated year, a correlation of 0.98 still left one stock 23% down and the other 0.2% up.

questions.prompt: Why can you rank pairs of stocks by correlation but not by covariance?
options: Correlation has no unit and always lies between -1 and 1
Correlation uses more days of data
Covariance ignores the sign of the moves
questions.explanation: Covariance grows with each stock's volatility, so wild pairs get big numbers. Dividing by both volatilities removes the units and puts every pair on the same -1 to 1 scale.
